cards.title: Live Auction Show Planning: Schedule Early, Promote Hard
cards.summary: Schedule live auction shows at least a week ahead and promote across channels to maximize bookmarks, which drives viewer turnout and higher average selling price.
cards.use_when: Planning a live-stream selling event (Whatnot or similar live auction) and deciding how far in advance to schedule and how to promote it.
steps: Schedule the show at least one week ahead, and two to three weeks out if possible, so the platform can remind bookmarked users when you go live.
Advertise the scheduled show on every channel you have: personal Facebook page, reseller Facebook groups, Instagram stories, and your YouTube videos.
Post promotion multiple times with escalating urgency: roughly one week before, two to three days before, and a few hours before the show.
Center the pre-show message on the quality of inventory and a reason to show up (for example 'high-quality inventory, all starting at $1'), not just the date.
Track bookmarks and max concurrent viewers as your feedback signal — the source's 530 max concurrent viewers (top-10 show in three years) was attributed to this multi-channel promotion.
caveats: The source's link between bookmarks and higher ASP is the seller's own experience, not a platform benchmark.
The presenter acknowledges their existing YouTube following helped; they also state sellers with no prior social following can grow purely inside the app.

cards.title: Thumbnail Design: Value Callouts and Brand Recognition
cards.summary: Build the show thumbnail in a free tool like Canva with the biggest incentive and recognizable brand names to win attention while viewers scroll.
cards.use_when: Creating the static thumbnail image for a live auction show listing on a platform where buyers scroll past many shows.
steps: Use a free design tool (the source used Canva) to make a simple static thumbnail.
Put the single biggest viewer incentive in large text — in the source's case 'Free iPad'.
List recognizable brand names of items being sold alongside their starting price, e.g. brands that would resell for $50–$150 on eBay, all starting at $1.
Keep the message consistent with your ad posts so anyone who saw the promo recognizes the show instantly.
Treat the thumbnail as a low-cost supporting asset: the source is unsure how much the thumbnail alone matters but argues it's worth making since you're already promoting heavily.
caveats: The source explicitly says they are not sure whether the thumbnail is 'super important' — treat it as a cheap complement to promotion, not a proven driver.

cards.title: Anchor High-Ticket Items Early to Shape Price Perception
cards.summary: Borrow Costco's front-of-store $5,000 TV logic: show your most expensive items first so everything after feels cheap and buyers bid more freely.
cards.use_when: Sequencing items during a live auction show or ordering products on a storefront/landing page to influence perceived value.
steps: Identify your highest-priced, most impressive items before the show starts.
Run or display those high-ticket anchor items early, mirroring how Costco puts the $5,000 flat-screen right at the entrance.
Let the rest of the catalog be perceived as comparatively affordable, which the source argues leads buyers to purchase more.
Segment the catalog: the source's show had ~50 high-value items ($50–$150 resale) meant to create excitement, and ~200 lower-cost items that carried the actual profit.
Accept that some anchor items may sell below eBay market value — that's the cost of the excitement they generate.
caveats: This is the presenter's analogy to observed retail practice, not a tested auction result.
You may lose money or margin on anchor items; plan the rest of the catalog's profitability accordingly.
cards.source_name: Our Secret Strategies to Making $975_Hour on Whatnot!.docx

cards.title: Use Loss Leaders and Freebies to Pull Buyers Toward Profitable Inventory
cards.summary: Make your money on the 80% of cheap, high-margin items while using giveaway-grade high-value items as the draw.
cards.use_when: Building a product mix for a live sale or promotion where you need traffic and engagement but profit comes from lower-cost goods.
steps: Identify a small share of your inventory that will be exciting but likely unprofitable (source: ~50 of 250 items, worth $50–$150, expected to sell below market).
Fill the majority of the show with low-cost goods you can buy cheaply and triple your money on — the source's normal shows buy at Goodwill bins or flea markets for $0.25–$5 and sell for $8–$15.
Use the loss-leader items purely as the hook that brings people in and keeps the room full; the source calls the leftover, already-paid-off inventory effectively 'free' cost of goods.
Recover the cost of a paid loss leader across the volume of the show: e.g., a $250 iPad is covered if each of ~250 items earns just one extra bid dollar.
caveats: The 'one extra dollar per item covers the iPad' arithmetic is the presenter's own framing example, not a guaranteed outcome.
Loss leaders can sell for far below market — the source saw this with Nike sneakers and motocross boots.
cards.source_name: Our Secret Strategies to Making $975_Hour on Whatnot!.docx

cards.title: Buyer Giveaway Mechanics: Reward Buyers, Incentivize Bids
cards.summary: Gate a giveaway to customers only (a 'buyer's giveaway') so it rewards purchases and nudges non-buyers to bid at least once.
cards.use_when: Designing a giveaway or incentive for a live-stream sale or event to convert viewers into buyers and lift purchase volume.
steps: Choose a giveaway prize large enough to motivate action — the source gave away an iPad, roughly $250.
Make the giveaway a 'buyer's giveaway': only people who made a purchase during the show can enter.
Run a small second giveaway early in the show (the source used Hello Kitty earrings) to spark engagement from the start, and save the bigger prize for the end.
Announce the giveaway in pre-show advertising so it also drives bookmarks.
Frame the math: if the prize makes each of N items earn an extra small bid, the prize pays for itself — the source felt their iPad did.
caveats: Whether the giveaway truly paid for itself is the presenter's own belief ('I think it worked'), not measured.
Prize cost is real cash outlay and must be included in your show's break-even calculation.
cards.source_name: Our Secret Strategies to Making $975_Hour on Whatnot!.docx

cards.title: Starting Bids at $1: When It Works and When It Doesn't
cards.summary: $1 starts create excitement only when the room is full; the source says most sellers should not use them.
cards.use_when: Deciding starting bid prices for auction inventory in a live-stream show.
steps: Reserve $1 starting bids for high-quality, recognizable items ($50–$150 resale value) — buyers ignore $1 starts on $5–$10 junk.
Only start at $1 if you expect a large, excited room; the source describes success with 300–500 concurrent viewers.
Publicize '$1 starts' in your advertising because it is a strong hook that drives bookmarks.
Accept the unpredictability: some $1-start items will sell below market and some far above; the source calls this the inherent nature of $1 auctions.
For normal shows without a big promoted audience, start higher — the source explicitly does not recommend $1 starts for most sellers.
caveats: The recommendation to avoid $1 starts for most sellers is the presenter's opinion, tied to room size.
No guaranteed price floor exists; losses on individual items are expected.
cards.source_name: Our Secret Strategies to Making $975_Hour on Whatnot!.docx

cards.title: Entertainment as Conversion: Costumes, Music, Energy
cards.summary: If viewers have fun they become buyers, and if buyers have fun they become repeat buyers — so build small bits into every show.
cards.use_when: Hosting a live-stream sale and trying to hold viewers, increase engagement, and improve conversion to purchase.
steps: Wear something visually distinct (a silly hat, viking helmet, shark costume); the source reports it becomes the main topic of chat every time and stands out while viewers scroll.
Play background music at low volume — not to entertain viewers but to make it easier for the seller to talk continuously and fill dead air.
Avoid silence: the source says doing literally nothing is the one thing to never do; dance, chat, or keep energy up.
Talk directly to new viewers in chat (ask first-timers to say hello) to make them feel included and more likely to buy.
Find a style that fits you — the source warns that forced comedy that the chat doesn't enjoy reads as 'cringe,' so play with it and adjust.
caveats: The source stresses entertainment style is highly individual; there is no universal script.
The buyer/repeat-buyer chain is the presenter's causal claim, not a measured funnel.
cards.source_name: Our Secret Strategies to Making $975_Hour on Whatnot!.docx

cards.title: Pacing a High-Volume Auction Show
cards.summary: Budget ~45 seconds to 1 minute per item and expect a 250-item show to run close to 4 hours.
cards.use_when: Planning show length, item count, and staffing for a live auction event.
steps: Estimate time per lot: the source's 252 items took 3 hours 57 minutes, roughly 45 seconds to 1 minute each.
Set a minimum countdown (their auctions start at 15 seconds) but let bids extend the timer when bidding continues.
Account for your own talking time — the source's show ran longer than planned (2.5–3 hours expected, ~4 actual) because of extended commentary and 'soap boxes'.
Plan capacity accordingly: staff shipping/replenishment so orders from a big show can be processed afterward (their helper took ~2 days, 6–7 paid hours at $25/hour).
Use the time-per-item figure to sanity-check whether a target item count is realistic for your show length.
caveats: Time per item is the source's own observed average, not a platform standard.
Sellers who talk more or less will see different totals.
cards.source_name: Our Secret Strategies to Making $975_Hour on Whatnot!.docx

cards.title: Calculate Show Profitability: Gross Sales, Fees, COGS
cards.summary: Track gross sales, platform fees and adjustments, inventory cost, and giveaway cost to get true show profit.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether a live-stream sale was actually profitable and planning break-even for the next show.
steps: Record gross sales for the show — the source's example: 252 items, $5,565 gross, ASP ~$22 (versus ~$9.85 in normal shows).
Subtract platform fees, shipping adjustments, and coupon/points redemptions to get actual payout — the source's example netted $4,006 from $5,565 gross.
Total your cost of goods: inventory purchases, the cost of any giveaway prize (iPad ~$250), and any included leftover stock you'd already paid off.
Add labor: the source counted ~6–7 hours of a helper at $25/hour for shipping, reducing profit from ~$3,900 to ~$3,750.
Set your break-even point: with ~$1,000 of inventory in, break-even was ~$1,000 in sales; everything above that was profit.
Win the show on a higher average selling price, not just item count — doubling ASP from ~$9.85 to ~$22 was the biggest single lever.
caveats: All figures are one seller's single show, not benchmarks or promises.
Fees, shipping adjustments and rewards deductions vary by platform and change over time — verify current fee structures.
cards.source_name: Our Secret Strategies to Making $975_Hour on Whatnot!.docx

cards.title: Read Show Health Metrics: Buyers, New Buyers, Concurrents
cards.summary: Use buyers-per-item, first-time buyers, max concurrent viewers, and total unique viewers to judge whether promotion worked.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a completed live sale to diagnose whether your promotion and show design succeeded and what to change next time.
steps: Count total buyers versus items sold to see repeat purchasing — the source sold 250 items to 153 buyers, indicating many multi-item buyers.
Track first-time buyers as a signal that promotion reached new audiences — 49 of the 153 were first-time buyers on the platform.
Track max concurrent viewers to gauge the peak of your audience — the source hit 530, among their top 10 shows in three years.
Track total unique viewers across the show — the source reached 6,158 people over ~4 hours, showing the platform's audience size.
Compare all of these against your normal, non-promoted shows to quantify the effect of the extra advertising effort.
caveats: These are the source's own single-show numbers, not benchmarks to target.
First-time buyer counts depend on platform tracking; verify how your platform reports them.
cards.source_name: Our Secret Strategies to Making $975_Hour on Whatnot!.docx

cards.title: Build Inventory Cheap to Protect Auction Margins
cards.summary: Source product from thrift bins, flea markets, and lot deals to keep COGS low enough that even $8–$15 sales are profitable.
cards.use_when: Sourcing inventory for a live auction or resale channel where per-item prices are low and volume is high.
steps: Buy from low-cost sources: thrift-store bins, flea markets, and bulk lots; the source buys at $0.25–$5 per item.
Look for bulk lot opportunities from other sellers — the source's friend offered 67 Funko Pops for $250 (~$4 per pop), which they considered a good deal.
Reuse already-paid-off inventory from previous events as effectively free cost of goods for the next show.
Aim for a consistent multiplier: the source targets roughly tripling money on low-cost items ($2 in, ~$8+ out) and relies on volume (about 150 items a week) for profitability.
Keep the show's total inventory cost low enough that break-even comes early — the source's $1,000-in / $1,000-out break-even for a 250-item show.
caveats: Low-cost sourcing is labor-intensive and depends on local supply; margins on tiny items are thin until moved at volume.
The source's sourcing channels (Goodwill bins, flea markets) are their own; other sources may yield different costs.
cards.source_name: Our Secret Strategies to Making $975_Hour on Whatnot!.docx

cards.title: Large Show vs. Routine Show: Match Format to Goal
cards.summary: Run small frequent shows for baseline cash and occasional big promoted shows with better inventory to lift ASP and reach new buyers.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to run a normal weekly live sale or invest in a larger, promoted event.
steps: In routine mode, run frequent smaller shows (the source does 2–3 per week with 30–50 items) as reliable baseline revenue.
In event mode, run a larger show (the source's 252 items) with higher-quality inventory and heavier promotion, accepting more planning and inventory outlay.
Use the event show to lift average selling price — the source went from ~$9.85 to ~$22 by combining better inventory, promotion, and excitement.
Accept more variability in a large show: some items sell below market and some above; the source says you 'never really know' with $1 starts.
Use the event to acquire new buyers who become followers for future routine shows.
caveats: Event shows demand more inventory capital, planning, and post-show shipping labor than routine shows.
The source notes not every seller can execute this format — it needs a full room and heavy promotion.
cards.source_name: Our Secret Strategies to Making $975_Hour on Whatnot!.docx

cards.title: Grow a Following Inside the Platform Without Off-Platform Audiences
cards.summary: A pre-existing social following helps but is not required — sellers can build audience directly on the selling platform.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest time in off-platform promotion or in-platform audience growth for a live-selling channel.
steps: Invest in the platform's own discovery tools: schedule shows, use strong thumbnails, promote within the app, and engage chat consistently.
Post show-to-show so repeat buyers keep coming back — the source credits the fun-buyer-repeat-buyer loop for channel growth.
Recognize that some highly successful sellers have no social media following and build entirely on-platform (the source cites sellers doing high volumes weekly with no external audience).
If you do have an off-platform following, use it as a multiplier for big events (the source attributes a top-10 show partly to YouTube and Instagram promotion).
Set expectations by category: routine small-show revenue versus large event revenue differ greatly — measure your own numbers rather than aiming at someone else's.
caveats: The source explicitly acknowledges their own YouTube following aided their results, so their outcomes are not directly reproducible without one.
High-revenue examples from other sellers are cited by the presenter as anecdotes, not audited figures.
